title: 7 Best Redwood Stain and Sealer Picks in 2026: Keep It Red
metaDescription: Penofin Blue Label is the best redwood stain and sealer for most decks. 7 picks, and why a redwood-toned finish keeps the color when a clear cannot.
h1: The 7 Best Redwood Stain and Sealer Picks in 2026

intro:
The best redwood stain and sealer for most decks, fences and siding is Penofin Blue Label, a penetrating oil that contractors on the West Coast have used on redwood for years: it soaks in, never peels and comes in transparent tones that keep the wood reading red. Ready Seal 520 Redwood is the easiest to apply well, and TWP 1500 and Sikkens Cetol SRD give the most protection in hard sun.

Redwood is bought for its color, and color is the first thing it loses. Sun breaks down the extractives that make it red within weeks, and rain washes them out. A clear sealer slows the water damage but not the fading. The seven finishes below are chosen for how well they keep redwood looking like redwood.
quickAnswer: Use a penetrating oil-based finish in a transparent redwood tone, not a clear. Penofin Blue Label is the best all-round choice, Ready Seal 520 Redwood is the most forgiving, TWP 1500 holds up best on sunny decks and DEFY Extreme is the water-based option. Clean gently, always brighten with oxalic acid and recoat every one to three years when water stops beading.

sections.body:

The core idea: to keep redwood red, use a finish that is a little red. A transparent redwood-toned finish blocks more UV than a clear and adds back color as it fades. For a wider list of pigmented finishes on every wood, see our [best deck stain rankings](/best-deck-stain-reviews/).

sections.heading: The 7 Best Redwood Stain and Sealer Picks in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
These are ranked from manufacturer data sheets and labels, the redwood-friendly tones each line offers, stated recoat guidance and recurring owner feedback on how each finish ages on redwood. No weathering trials were run for this guide, and no brand paid for placement. Products that maintain with a cleaning and a fresh coat rank above ones that need stripping.

### Best Overall: Penofin Blue Label Penetrating Oil Finish
Penofin has deep roots on the West Coast, where redwood decks and siding are common, and Blue Label is the product many contractors reach for on redwood. The company describes it as an oil-based finish built around Brazilian rosewood oil, and it soaks into redwood rather than sitting on top. That means it does not peel: when it wears, the wood looks drier and lighter, and a cleaning and fresh coat bring it back. The line includes a clear and several transparent tones, and picking a redwood-friendly tone is what keeps boards from fading toward tan. It works on decks, siding, fences and furniture, so one product can cover the whole property. Apply thin, back-brush and wipe off what does not absorb. Owners often comment on how natural it looks next to heavier stains. The cautions are standard for oils: longer dry times, mineral-spirits cleanup and some formulas restricted in low-VOC areas.

**Pros:** Contractor favorite on redwood; penetrates without a film; redwood-friendly transparent tones; recoats with cleaning only; works on decks, siding and fences.
**Cons:** Solvent cleanup; some formulas restricted in low-VOC areas; excess must be wiped.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Penofin+Blue+Label+penetrating+oil+finish+redwood&tag=sktiger-20)

### Easiest to Apply: Ready Seal 520 Redwood Exterior Stain and Sealer
Ready Seal 520 is the brand's redwood tone, made for owners who want the job to be easy. Ready Seal markets the formula as needing no back-brushing and leaving no lap marks, and owner feedback largely agrees: people who fought streaky finishes before often say Ready Seal looked even on the first try. You can spray, roll or brush it, which helps on long fences and big decks. The redwood tint adds color back, blocks UV and evens out sapwood and heartwood better than a clear. It looks lighter when wet and deepens over roughly two weeks as it cures, so judge the color after that. On very pale sapwood it can look stronger than on red heartwood; test a board first. Maintenance is simple: clean and recoat when water stops beading.

**Pros:** Redwood tone made for the species; no back-brushing or lap marks per maker; spray, roll or brush; fades instead of peeling; sold in five-gallon pails.
**Cons:** Color develops over two weeks; slower drying than water-based; strong on pale sapwood.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ready+Seal+520+Redwood+stain+and+sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Most Durable Oil: TWP 1500 Series Wood Preservative
TWP 1500 is a penetrating oil that the company positions as a wood preservative, with mildew resistance noted on the label. Restoration contractors like it because it soaks into weathered wood and fades rather than peeling, so recoats are a cleaning and a fresh coat. The line includes redwood and cedar tones, and that pigment keeps redwood from fading quickly. On sunny redwood decks, owners often report it holds color longer than clear products, though traffic lanes still need attention every year or two. It handles rough, weathered boards well, filling the texture instead of sitting on it. The trade-offs are availability, since many buyers order online, and patience: it needs warm, dry weather to cure. Test the tone on a board first.

**Pros:** Preservative with mildew resistance; redwood and cedar tones; penetrates weathered wood; recoats without stripping.
**Cons:** Restricted in some low-VOC states; often ordered online; longer cure.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=TWP+1500+Series+redwood+wood+preservative&tag=sktiger-20)

### Richest Color: Cabot Australian Timber Oil
Cabot Australian Timber Oil is a translucent oil finish known for rich color. It was designed with dense hardwoods in mind but works on redwood and cedar too, and many redwood owners choose it for the depth it adds to the grain, an almost furniture-like look when first applied. Because it penetrates instead of forming a film, it fades gradually and refreshes after cleaning. It is stocked at major retailers, which makes touch-ups easy. The main caution is color: some tones read orange or very dark on pale sapwood, so test on a hidden board and judge it in sunlight. Wipe off what the wood does not absorb, since excess stays tacky. It is also a good clear-ish answer for redwood outdoor furniture and picnic tables, applied in thin coats.

**Pros:** Rich translucent color; penetrates hard and soft woods; easy to find; no film to peel.
**Cons:** Some tones read orange on pale wood; longer dry times; excess must be wiped.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Cabot+Australian+Timber+Oil&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Semi-Transparent: Sikkens ProLuxe Cetol SRD
Sikkens ProLuxe Cetol SRD has a long reputation on cedar and redwood, especially in sunny regions. The maker describes it as a one-coat, penetrating, semi-transparent stain, and it relies on transparent iron oxide pigments to block UV while letting the grain show. That gives it more sun protection than the lighter penetrating oils, at the cost of a slightly darker, more stain-like look. It suits redwood decks and siding that face south or west, and older redwood that needs more color to look even. Owners commonly say it holds color well on vertical surfaces, with traffic areas on floors needing touch-ups over time. It is sold mainly through paint stores and online and costs more per gallon than big-box finishes.

**Pros:** One coat per the maker; transparent iron oxides for UV; long record on redwood; works on decks, siding and fences.
**Cons:** Paint stores and online only; higher price; darker than penetrating oils.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Sikkens+ProLuxe+Cetol+SRD&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Water-Based: DEFY Extreme Semi-Transparent Wood Stain
DEFY Extreme is a water-based finish that uses zinc oxide nanoparticles and pigment to resist UV. For redwood owners its advantages are practical: soap-and-water cleanup, low odor, fast drying and legal sale in states with strict VOC limits where some oils are not available. The line includes redwood-friendly tones, and the semi-transparent pigment helps keep the red from fading. It penetrates rather than building a heavy film, so wear shows as fading. It wants warm, dry weather with no dew while it dries, and owners note it can look flatter than an oil on redwood, without the warm glow oil gives the grain. Expect recoats every year or two on sunny decks and longer on siding.

**Pros:** Low odor, water cleanup; zinc oxide UV resistance; redwood tones; fast drying; sold where oils are restricted.
**Cons:** Needs warm, dry curing weather; flatter look than oil; shorter life on very sunny decks.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DEFY+Extreme+semi-transparent+wood+stain+redwood&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Big-Box Pick: Olympic Maximum Stain + Sealant in One, Semi-Transparent
Olympic Maximum is the mainstream semi-transparent finish at Lowe's, and it suits redwood owners who want to buy locally and have the color tinted in store. The label promises water repellency and a mildew-resistant finish, and the semi-transparent pigment helps redwood hold color better than a clear. The same line includes clear, transparent, semi-transparent and solid versions, so you can change the look later without switching brands. Owners commonly report good results on fences and siding and more frequent touch-ups on sunny decks. Because it behaves somewhat more like a coating than a pure penetrating oil, repeated heavy coats can build up, so apply thin and only recoat once water soaks in again.

**Pros:** Tinted at Lowe's; stain and sealant in one; mildew-resistant finish per label; redwood-friendly colors; moderate price.
**Cons:** Can build up with repeated coats; less natural than penetrating oils; shorter life on sunny floors.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Olympic+Maximum+stain+and+sealant+semi-transparent&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Why Does Redwood Lose Its Color So Fast?
sections.body:
### Sun breaks down the extractives
Redwood heartwood gets its color and much of its decay resistance from extractives, including tannins, concentrated near the surface of a fresh board. Ultraviolet light breaks them down within weeks of exposure, and a new deck can look noticeably paler by its first fall.

### Rain carries them away
Water leaches the broken-down extractives out of the surface, sometimes leaving dark brown streaks where it runs or pools. Over time the surface goes from red to tan to silver gray.

### Why clear sealers disappoint
A clear sealer keeps rain from soaking in and leaching extractives, and it reduces checking and cupping. It does very little about UV, so the color still fades. That is why clear redwood finishes so often let owners down.

### Pigment changes the outcome
A finish with transparent red or brown iron oxide pigment blocks a share of UV at the surface and replaces some of the color the sun takes. The finish fades instead of the wood, and a maintenance coat restores it.

### Climate sets the pace
In coastal fog, redwood fades slowly and mildew is the bigger threat. At altitude or in desert sun, a new deck can lose most of its red in one summer. South- and west-facing boards and stair treads fade first.

sections.heading: Should You Use a Clear Sealer or a Redwood-Toned Stain?
sections.body:
### Clear
Choose clear only if you like redwood's natural shift toward tan or gray and want to keep the wood dry while it happens. Clears suit covered porches and furniture that see little direct sun. On an open deck, plan on a yearly recoat. Our [deck sealant guide](/best-deck-sealant/) covers clear water repellents.

### Redwood tone
The default for most owners. It adds back warm color, blocks more UV than a clear and evens out pale sapwood. Freshly coated boards look a little more saturated than bare new redwood.

### Cedar or natural tones
Lighter tints for a more golden, less red look, or for faded redwood you do not want to push back to red. They still add UV protection.

### Darker semi-transparent
Deeper tones hide weathering, mismatched boards and old stains and last longer in heavy sun, but cover more of the wood's character.

| Finish look | UV protection | Best for | Typical recoat |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Clear | Low | Covered areas, furniture | About yearly |
| Redwood toned | Moderate | Most decks and siding | 1 to 3 years |
| Cedar or natural toned | Moderate | Faded redwood, lighter look | 1 to 3 years |
| Darker semi-transparent | Higher | Weathered or mixed boards | 2 to 4 years |

sections.heading: Why Do Redwood Boards Look Mismatched?
sections.body:
### Heartwood and sapwood
Redwood boards come from two parts of the tree. Heartwood, from the center, is the red, decay-resistant wood most people picture. Sapwood, from the outer rings, is cream to pale yellow and has much less natural rot resistance. Grades that allow sapwood show both colors side by side.

### Grade names
Heartwood-only grades are commonly sold under names such as clear all heart or construction heart, while grades with sapwood are often labeled construction common or carry a B prefix. Names vary by mill and region, so ask.

### Even it out with a toned finish
A redwood or cedar tint darkens pale sapwood more than red heartwood, narrowing the contrast. A pure clear does the opposite and highlights the difference.

### Protect the sapwood
Sapwood is less durable. Pay extra attention to coverage and drainage, and brush an end-cut preservative onto cut ends during construction. Many redwood decks also sit on pressure-treated framing; if any treated boards show, our guide to the [best stain for pressure treated wood](/best-deck-stain-for-pressure-treated-wood/) covers them.

sections.heading: How Do You Clean and Brighten Redwood Before Sealing?
sections.body:
### Clean gently
Use an oxygen-based deck cleaner, which relies on sodium percarbonate to lift dirt and mildew without the fiber damage chlorine bleach causes. Wet the wood, apply the cleaner, let it work for the label time and scrub with a stiff synthetic brush.

### Rinse at low pressure
Use a garden hose or a pressure washer at low pressure with a wide fan tip. Redwood is soft; a narrow, high-pressure stream raises fuzz and carves the earlywood into a washboard that absorbs unevenly. A [surface cleaner attachment](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/) spreads the force evenly on big floors.

### Always brighten
Cleaners are alkaline and darken redwood. An oxalic acid brightener lowers the pH, restores much of the red and removes the blue-black stains that form when iron from steel fasteners or tools reacts with tannins.

### Keep iron away
Use stainless steel fasteners on visible redwood; hot-dip galvanized is acceptable in many places, but stainless is safer. Avoid steel wool and plain steel brushes.

### Let it dry
Allow 24 to 48 hours of dry weather. A water drop that soaks in within a minute or two shows the surface is open and ready.

sections.heading: How Do You Restore Gray Redwood and Seal It?
sections.body:
### Gray is usually only skin deep
The gray is a thin layer of weathered fibers; the red heartwood beneath is still there. A cleaner followed by a brightener removes much of it, and a redwood-toned finish brings the color back. It will not look brand new, but it gets close.

### Strip peeling films first
If an old film finish is peeling, remove it with a stripper rated for that finish, then brighten. Avoid aggressive coarse-grit sanding, which removes the layer that holds color.

### Clear up stubborn stains
Black streaks that survive cleaning are often iron stains; a second targeted pass of oxalic acid usually removes them. Mildew that returns quickly points to shade and poor airflow, so trim plants and clear board gaps.

### Check the structure
Push a screwdriver into boards near the house, around posts and on stairs. Soft spots mean decay, more common in sapwood. Replace those boards with heartwood if you can.

### Apply thin
Pick a mild, dry day, roughly 50 to 90 degrees Fahrenheit, with the boards out of midday sun. Coat two or three boards at a time along their full length, back-brush, and wipe up anything not absorbed in the label's wait time. Do railings and vertical parts first, then the floor. Mix all cans in one bucket first so the color stays even, and dry oily rags flat outdoors. Our [deck stain drying time guide](/deck-stain-drying-time/) covers rain and foot-traffic windows.

sections.heading: How Do You Seal a Redwood Fence, Siding or Furniture?
sections.body:
### Fences
Redwood fences are vertical, so a toned finish lasts well. Large fences are easiest to spray, so choose a product that tolerates spraying without lap marks, such as Ready Seal. Our [fence stain guide](/best-fence-stain/) ranks products for long runs.

### Siding
Redwood siding sheds water and gets angled sun, so it lasts longest between coats. A toned penetrating oil can go several years on shaded walls; sunny elevations need more frequent coats. The [exterior wood sealer guide](/best-exterior-wood-sealer/) covers products made for vertical wood.

### Furniture and picnic tables
Redwood furniture is softer than teak and takes standard penetrating finishes. For a good clear-looking finish on a picnic table, use a thin coat of a penetrating oil in a clear or light tone and wipe off the excess so nothing stays tacky. Expect to refresh it every year.

### Planters, hot tubs and wet areas
Finish only the outside of planters and use a liner inside. Redwood around hot tubs and pools stays wet often, so clean it more often and recoat when water stops beading.

### Rain and snow country
To protect redwood against rain and snow and prevent drying and splintering, keep a penetrating finish in good condition rather than building thick films, which crack in freeze-thaw. Recoat on schedule and keep snow shovels plastic.

sections.heading: How Much Redwood Sealer Do You Need, and How Often Should You Reseal?
sections.body:
### Coverage
Most penetrating redwood finishes list roughly 150 to 300 square feet per gallon per coat on smooth wood, and less on rough or weathered boards. A first coat after restoration takes more than a maintenance coat. Measure decking, railings and stairs separately.

### Recoat interval
Most redwood decks need a fresh coat every one to three years depending on sun, climate, traffic and the finish. Clears often need yearly attention; toned and semi-transparent finishes last longer. Siding and fences go longer.

### The spring and fall check
Do the water-drop test each spring and fall. When water soaks in on the sunniest boards, clean, brighten and recoat. With penetrating finishes you can recoat just the stairs and traffic paths and the new coat blends in.

### Do not stack coats
Never add a coat to wood that still beads water. The new finish cannot penetrate, sits on top and turns sticky and dark, which is the most common redwood finish complaint.

### Keep a record
Stay with the same product and tone, and write down the product, tone and date. If you hire out, get the brand and tone in writing and confirm the crew uses low pressure and a brightener.

mistakes.title: Waiting a year to seal new redwood
mistakes.body: Redwood loses much of its red in the first months of sun, so waiting a full season means sealing wood that has already faded. Unless the boards are wet or glazed, clean and finish new redwood once it is dry and absorbs water, often within a few weeks.

mistakes.title: Using steel wool or plain steel fasteners
mistakes.body: Iron reacts with redwood tannins and leaves blue-black stains, especially after rain. Use stainless steel fasteners and synthetic scrub pads, and remove existing iron stains with an oxalic acid brightener before sealing.

mistakes.title: Pressure washing at high pressure
mistakes.body: Redwood is soft, and a narrow, high-pressure stream raises fuzz and gouges the earlywood. The damaged surface absorbs finish unevenly and looks blotchy. Let the cleaner work, keep pressure low, use a wide fan tip and hold the wand well back.

mistakes.title: Choosing a clear finish to keep the red
mistakes.body: Clear finishes keep redwood dry but do little against UV, so the red still fades to tan and gray. If color is the goal, use a redwood-toned or semi-transparent finish with transparent pigment and refresh it when water stops beading.

mistakes.title: Skipping the brightener after cleaning
mistakes.body: Deck cleaners are alkaline and leave redwood darker and duller. Skipping the oxalic acid brightener seals in that dull color and any iron stains. A brightener restores much of the red and neutralizes the cleaner so the finish looks right and bonds well.

faqs.q: What is the best redwood stain and sealer?
faqs.a: Penofin Blue Label is the best redwood stain and sealer for most decks, fences and siding because it penetrates without peeling and comes in transparent redwood tones. Ready Seal 520 Redwood is the easiest to apply, TWP 1500 is the most durable oil and Sikkens Cetol SRD gives the most UV protection.

faqs.q: What is the best clear sealer for redwood?
faqs.a: For a clear look, Penofin Blue Label in its clear version or a thin coat of Cabot Australian Timber Oil are good choices, since both penetrate instead of peeling. Expect yearly recoats, because clears block little UV. If you want to keep the red color, a transparent redwood tone works much better.

Not strictly, but it is wise. Redwood heartwood resists decay naturally and can survive unsealed, but it will turn gray and check over time. Sealing slows water absorption, cracking and mildew, and a toned finish keeps the red color. Sapwood boards and decks in wet climates benefit most.

faqs.q: How do you seal a redwood fence?
faqs.a: Clean the fence with an oxygen cleaner, rinse at low pressure, apply an oxalic acid brightener and let it dry for 24 to 48 hours. Then spray or brush a penetrating redwood-toned finish such as Ready Seal 520 or Penofin, back-brushing as you go and wiping off excess. Recoat every few years.

faqs.q: How do you get the red color back on gray redwood?
faqs.a: Clean with an oxygen-based deck cleaner, rinse at low pressure and apply an oxalic acid brightener, which restores much of the red and removes iron stains. Once the wood is dry, apply a redwood-toned penetrating finish. The color will not match brand-new boards exactly but comes close.

faqs.q: Is oil or water-based sealer better for redwood?
faqs.a: Oil-based penetrating finishes are usually preferred on redwood because they soak in, enrich the color and fade gradually. Water-based finishes such as DEFY Extreme dry faster, smell less, clean up with water and are legal in strict VOC states. Both work if the wood is cleaned and brightened first.

faqs.q: How often should a redwood deck be resealed?
faqs.a: Most redwood decks need a fresh coat every one to three years, depending on sun, climate, foot traffic and the finish. Clear finishes often need yearly attention, while toned or semi-transparent finishes last longer. Use the water-drop test each spring and recoat when water soaks in.

bottomLine: Penofin Blue Label is the redwood finish to start with, and Ready Seal 520 Redwood is the easiest to apply well. TWP 1500 and Sikkens Cetol SRD give more protection in harsh sun, Cabot Australian Timber Oil gives the richest color, DEFY Extreme is the water-based choice and Olympic Maximum is the easy local buy. Whichever you choose, the method matters as much as the can: clean gently, brighten, keep iron away from the wood, use a toned finish rather than a clear and recoat when water stops beading. For more penetrating oils, see our [oil-based deck stain picks](/best-oil-based-deck-stain/).
